argv:
import asyncio
import sys
from mcp import ClientSession, StdioServerParameters
from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client

async def main():
    parameters = StdioServerParameters(
        command=sys.executable,
        args=["-m", "pyocd_debug_mcp.server"],
    )
    async with stdio_client(parameters) as streams:
        async with ClientSession(*streams) as session:
            await session.initialize()
            tools = (await session.list_tools()).tools
            names = {tool.name for tool in tools}
            assert "initialization_handshake" in names
            print(f"stdio tool count: {len(names)}")

asyncio.run(main())

acceptance.description: Calling the handshake returns guidance containing every element listed under Outputs (verifiable by inspection of the returned text).
The handshake action is visible and callable at the start of every Server Run before any other action has been called.
Calling or not calling the handshake produces no difference in any subsequent authorization decision (locked tools remain locked either way).
The guidance explicitly instructs the agent never to expose structured payloads, continuation tokens, or internal field names to the user.
At every Server Run start, board-specific actions fail until the naming/assignment flow has produced a one-to-one mapping for the targeted board.
The Server enumerates every physical connection separately and provides friendly, human-relayable descriptions for each.
A user-supplied name matching exactly one existing profile routes to validation only — never to first-time setup.
A name matching no profile routes to the setup-plan flow; a profile with recorded incomplete/failed setup routes to the repair flow.
Assigning one board identity to two active connections, or two identities to one connection, is rejected.
On a reported hardware/profile mismatch, no profile content changes; the only path forward offered is correcting the assignment.
All assignments are in-memory: after Server restart, no assignment survives.
At Server Run start, every always-guarded action is absent from the tool list AND returns a failure if called by name.
After a valid plan is accepted, the underlying action appears in the tool list and is callable for exactly that board with exactly the planned parameters.
Unlocking is never achieved by tool-list manipulation alone: a hidden tool called directly (bypassing the list) still fails until its plan/permission conditions are met.
When a plan is exhausted, replaced, or invalidated, its underlying action is removed from the tool list (unless another active plan exposes it) and calls to it fail.
All unlocks reset when the Server Run ends: a new Server Run starts with the default visibility and lock state.
A failure returned for a locked action names the prerequisite (`*-plan` tool, setup, validation, or permission) required to proceed.
A populated plan submitted before the all-`NULL` call for that plan tool in the current Server Run is rejected with instructions to make the all-`NULL` call.
The all-`NULL` response contains every element listed under Outputs.
A plan missing any required field, or with `hypothesis_made`/`strategy_evaluated` not `true`, or with empty reasoning text, is rejected.
A plan for a fixed-budget action with any budget other than `1,0` is rejected.
A valid plan unlocks exactly one underlying tool for exactly one board, and the response includes plan identifier, underlying tool name, total calls, and a redirect instruction.
Calling the underlying tool with any parameter differing from the plan is rejected and consumes no budget.
An underlying call that starts and then fails or is cancelled still consumes one budgeted call.
When the budget reaches zero, the underlying tool relocks and further calls fail; a replacement plan is required.
Submitting a new valid plan for the same tool+board closes the prior plan; calls under the prior plan's parameters fail thereafter.
No plan survives a Server restart.
A permission-locked plan with no valid permission and no active full-session grant is rejected with a permission request.
`one-time` permission with a plan budget other than `1,0` is rejected.
After one accepted underlying call under `one-time` permission, the next attempt requires a new plan with new permission.
After `full-session` is granted for tool+board, a later valid plan with `user_permission = NULL` succeeds for that tool+board, and the all-`NULL` response discloses the active grant.
Full-session permission for one tool+board has no effect on any other tool or board.
All permissions are void after the Server Run ends.
Mass-erase operations request fresh user permission on every occurrence, even under an existing full-session grant.
A profile artifact whose storage name does not match its internal board identifier is rejected wherever it is read, with a clear error.
Creating a second profile with an existing display name is rejected.
After a successful live connection, the core profile fields listed above are persisted; before it, none are.
Optional enrichment fields appear in a profile only after their live validation passed; failed candidates appear only in reports.
No sequence of agent tool calls can result in a persisted artifact containing an agent-supplied value that the Server did not deterministically validate.
The MCU part number in a committed profile always equals the value the user supplied (or the known-board definition they selected), regardless of any research or detection outcome.
Device-support package metadata appears in exactly one manifest artifact and in no profile.
`board_setup` and `board_fix_setup` are callable only after a valid, permitted setup plan, and at most once each per plan.
With no probe attached, setup terminates deterministically with the no-probe status and no research prompt is issued.
Every ambiguity in the preflight table resolves through the stated deterministic or conversational path; the Server never guesses among multiple probes, ports, or build configurations.
After a failed `board_setup`, one `board_fix_setup` succeeds or fails under the same plan without any new user prompt; the second repair attempt is impossible without a replacement plan.
Every setup or repair attempt — successful or not — produces a persisted structured report with all listed content.
Setup completion relocks both setup actions and is followed by validation before any gate opens.
Repair never skips re-verification: recorded phase results are re-checked against live preflight before being reused.
Every research-required response contains all elements listed under Outputs.
A research reply containing fields not requested by the prompt is rejected.
A research reply attempting to alter the MCU part number is rejected and the part number remains unchanged everywhere.
A byte-identical resubmission of a previously failed candidate is rejected without a fresh validation attempt, and the subsequent prompt lists the prior failure.
No research acceptance, by itself, changes any gate, unlock, or permission state.
A locked target or missing probe produces a blocked status, not a research prompt.
When exactly one exact target is auto-detected, no target research prompt is issued.
A proposed target is committed to the profile only after a successful live connection using it.
A staged package failing checksum comparison (when an official checksum exists) is rejected and not promoted.
A staged package that does not expose the requested target is rejected with the observed target listing recorded.
A failed enrichment candidate is absent from the profile and present in the report with evidence, observed output, and candidate fingerprint.
Core setup can complete without optional enrichment when required identity checks pass.
Before `safety_setup_completed`, every write-capable hardware action for that board fails closed.
A doubly verified region is accepted only when both sources agree (or reconcile deterministically); a disagreement yields `safety_setup_conflict` and the affected actions stay closed.
Application and bootloader partitions in the map always come from the selected build/link artifacts, never from device documentation or agent assertion.
An address inside a prohibited region is denied for every request type even if it also falls inside a peripheral, flash, or RAM classification.
A request touching any address absent from the map is denied.
The persisted map contains per-source fingerprints and an aggregate fingerprint, and records each region's verification/derivation provenance.
A change to any fingerprinted source closes the affected board's gate before the next write-capable action executes.
After a build-artifact-only change, a successful refresh reopens the gate without any reconnection or re-validation, and only build-derived regions are rebuilt.
A part-number or target change makes refresh insufficient: the gate reopens only after full safety setup and validation.
`refresh_scope_unclear` never reopens the gate; it directs to full safety setup.
After a disconnect, no sequence of refresh calls reopens the gate without a successful `board_validate` on the reconnected assignment.
Freshness checks run on every write-capable guarded call, and a stale result blocks the call with the applicable required action named.
A successful validation opens exactly one gate — the validated board's — and stamps it with that connection's identity and the current aggregate fingerprint.
Each of the seven result statuses is produced under its stated condition and no other.
Validation makes no persistent changes to profiles or maps and performs no write, flash, or recovery operation on the board.
Every validation attempt, pass or fail, persists a report and log.
With a live MCU identity mismatch, validation fails and the profile remains unmodified; the only offered remedies are correcting the physical assignment or attaching the correct board.
At every Server Run start and for every new connection, all gates are closed.
There exists no tool call whose sole function is "open gate."
Disconnecting a board immediately closes its gate and clears its assignment and validation stamp, even mid-workflow.
Restarting the Server with all artifacts intact still requires naming, assignment, and validation before any guarded write on any board.
Each closed-gate rejection names the correct reopening path per the matrix above.
Every Layer 2 action requires and honors a board identity parameter; a request reaches only that board's assigned connection (observable with two boards attached).
Every Layer 2 response includes both the operation result and a safe-exit reminder.
`write_memory` with a raw address and no fallback flag is rejected with the symbol-first guidance; with the flag but no reason it is rejected; with flag + reason it succeeds only inside mapped RAM.
A `flash_application` artifact with any loadable segment outside the application partition is rejected before any erase or write occurs.
`flash_bootloader` without an approved permission-carrying plan returns a failure directing to `flash_bootloader-plan`.
A `register_write` whose range crosses into a prohibited subrange is rejected even if it begins inside a valid peripheral window.
`write_cpu_register` rejects control-flow/mode registers; `set_execution_state` accepts them only with permission; both reject names unsupported by the connected core.
`set_breakpoint` rejects addresses outside mapped executable regions.
`read_serial` and `write_serial` reject non-positive durations/timeouts and non-positive baud rates.
An erase implied by flashing never touches sectors outside the named partition.
Reset actions never change a locked target's security state.
A `target_unlock-plan` with any budget other than `1,0` is rejected.
The permission request contains every element in the Outputs list, including concrete erase ranges.
A full-chip-erase-only device produces a permission request explicitly stating total nonvolatile erasure.
Resubmitting the plan with any field changed after approval is rejected; the approval does not transfer.
A second mass erase in the same Server Run under any prior grant still triggers a fresh permission request.
Changing the target, probe, safety map, or plan between approval and execution invalidates the approval.
After `target_unlock` executes, no guarded write is possible until validation passes again.
No parameterization of `target_unlock` performs a write to security/provisioning registers outside the documented vendor recovery operation.
A batch containing children with two different board identities is rejected before any child runs.
A batch containing a batch is rejected.
A guarded child without an active covering plan causes that child to fail exactly as a direct call would.
Gate closure between children (e.g., disconnect mid-batch) blocks subsequent write-capable children.
Children execute strictly in listed order.
Killing the client mid-operation results, within a bounded time, in: serial port closed, debug session closed, helper work terminated, board lock released.
A cancelled non-flash operation stops promptly and its resources are freed; a subsequent operation on the same board succeeds without manual intervention.
A cancelled in-progress flash completes the flash before releasing resources; the written firmware is complete and bootable.
An operation exceeding its timeout is terminated and cleaned up identically to a cancellation.
Two concurrent operations on one probe/board never interleave; the second waits or fails busy.
A failing finalizer does not prevent any mandatory cleanup step.
A finalizer request specifying anything outside the documented structured whitelist is rejected at call time.
After an unclean previous run, a new Server Run starts successfully and cleans up the leftovers.
After the user confirms an ambiguous adapter once, an identical hardware arrangement in a later Server Run resolves without re-asking.
A port-path change alone (same stable identities) does not re-prompt.
Any of the ignore conditions (missing identity, changed hardware, multiple matches, different probe, revocation) causes a conversational re-confirmation instead of silent reuse.
The cache file is absent from version-control tracking in a freshly initialized project.
With two boards attached and only board A validated, every guarded action naming board B fails while the same action naming board A succeeds.
A plan created for board A does not unlock the underlying action for board B.
Disconnecting board A closes only board A's gate; board B's open gate and active plans are unaffected.
Full-session permission granted for a tool on board A does not satisfy the permission requirement for the same tool on board B.

cross_cutting.description: The Server serves exactly one local client on one computer, with no authentication and no network exposure. It must be unreachable from other machines.
Tool visibility is never authorization; every hidden tool is also functionally locked (AC-3.3).
Unknown memory is denied by default for every operation; prohibited classifications override all broader classifications.
The agent has no path to: persist state directly, supply allowed ranges, alter the user's part number, or open any gate (AC-6.5, AC-8.3, AC-8.5).
No tool accepts arbitrary shell commands, including cleanup/finalizer parameters (AC-17.7).
Security/provisioning regions and mass erase are unavailable to ordinary workflows; mass erase requires fresh, range-disclosing user permission every time (AC-5.7, AC-15.2).

All server-originated content intended for the user is plain prose suitable for verbatim conversational relay; every response that requires user input or research includes an explicit instruction to the agent not to expose structured payloads, continuation tokens, or internal field names.
There is no user-facing terminal-command layer and no separate research provider.

The Server interoperates with standard tool-calling agent clients (see Assumption A-1), including honoring client-issued request cancellation where the client sends it, and behaving safely (via timeouts and deterministic cleanup) where the client does not (see Open Question Q-1).
Gate/freshness checks add no more than 250 ms to a guarded call on a typical developer workstation.
Hardware enumeration at startup completes within 10 seconds for up to 8 attached probes/ports.
The all-`NULL` plan response and initialization handshake return within 2 seconds.
Every operation has a finite timeout; no tool call can hang a Server Run indefinitely (AC-17.4).

No single action available without destructive-recovery permission can leave the MCU permanently unrecoverable; application/bootloader crashes must remain recoverable through the Server's own reset/flash actions.
After any operation ends by any path, the next operation can reconnect without manual host intervention (AC-17.1–AC-17.5).
Profiles: created by setup, updated only by Server actions after validation, user-deletable as files; deleting a profile makes its name unknown at next resolution (routes to setup).
Reports/logs: one immutable structured record per setup/validation attempt; failures, research exchanges, and fingerprint changes are always recorded.
Cache: revocable and regenerable at any time with no effect on profiles.
No secret material is persisted; nothing in the artifact store grants authority (artifacts never restore an open gate — AC-13.4).
The product's entire human interface is conversational text relayed by the agent; no requirement in this specification depends on a graphical interface, color, sound, or pointing device.

All user-relayable text is in clear, jargon-minimal language; hardware choices are described by human-friendly distinguishing features (e.g., probe identifier endings), never raw internal identifiers alone.
Initial release is English-only (Decision A-17; see Q-6). Display names supplied by the user may contain non-ASCII characters and must round-trip losslessly.
